page: Amazon Web Services m6a.xlarge is a general-purpose instance based on the AWS Nitro System and powered by an AMD EPYC 7R13 processor running at 3.6 GHz. The virtual machine provides 4 vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores using simultaneous multithreading, coupled with dedicated CPU allocation. It is configured with 16.0 GB of DDR4 system memory running at 3 GHz, delivering a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. Hardware acceleration is limited to standard x86 extensions such as AVX, AES-NI, and SHA-NI, with no AVX-512 support. The instance includes 2 Gbps of baseline networking bandwidth and features no bundled local instance storage or discrete GPUs.

Benchmark results highlight strong single-core performance, evidenced by a stress-ng single-core score of 2991.79 placing it in the top quartile. Single-threaded metrics remain consistent across standard suites, yielding an average Geekbench single-core score of 1633.0 and an overall PassMark CPU score of 6837.73. Conversely, parallel execution reflects the instance's 4-vCPU ceiling, showing lower multi-core performance in stress-ng (5981.17) and Geekbench multi-core (3703.0). Memory throughput metrics demonstrate typical DDR4 limits, with uncached read speeds reaching 37.49 GB/sec and write bandwidth peaking at 22.1 GB/sec. Redis execution achieves 4.52 million SET operations per second, while static web serving throughput caps at 5.5 GB/sec.

The hardware configuration offers a cost-efficient profile for general workloads that do not require specialized accelerators or high disk throughput. Because the instance has no local ephemeral storage, persistent and scratch volumes require remote Elastic Block Store allocation. Given the balanced memory-to-vCPU ratio and reliable single-thread compute capabilities, m6a.xlarge is suited for standard web serving, application backends, containerized microservices, build nodes in CI/CD pipelines, and medium-scale caching or queuing layers.
description: Amazon Web Services m6a.xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the AWS Nitro System and powered by a 3.6 GHz AMD EPYC 7R13 processor. It provides 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores with dedicated allocation, paired with 16.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, maintaining a balanced 1:4 core-to-memory ratio. The instance includes 2 Gbps of baseline network bandwidth and operates without local storage or discrete GPU accelerators. Benchmark evaluations show strong single-core compute performance in stress-ng tests alongside average results across Geekbench single-core and PassMark CPU suites. However, multi-core throughput and memory bandwidth benchmarks fall into lower percentile tiers due to the constrained core count. Given its balanced resource distribution, lack of AVX-512 support, and reliance on remote block storage, m6a.xlarge is cost-effective for standard production workloads, such as containerized microservices, small-to-medium relational web backends, CI/CD worker nodes, and mid-tier enterprise application hosting.
